Science in Qumran Aramaic Texts by Ida Fröhlich

Ancient Cultures of Sciences and Knowledge 1. Tübingen: Mohr Siebeck, 2022. Pp. xii + 262. ISBN 978–3–16–161387–6/eISBN 978–3–16–161388–3. Paper/eBook €99.00

Reviewed by Joe Morgan Currie Harvard University joecurrie@g.harvard.edu

Science in Qumran Aramaic Texts primarily explores the astronomical, de­ monological, divinatory, and medical imaginations of the Aramaic texts found at Khirbet Qumran (e.g., 4Q242, 4Q208–209, and 4Q560), in the He­ brew Bible (Daniel 5), and in Ge’ez translations (e.g., the Book of the Watchers and the Astronomical Book of 1 Enoch). If there is a core argument to the volume, it is that these understudied and fragmentary Aramaic texts must be analyzed on their own terms as witnesses to a distinct scientific tradition. They must not be thoughtlessly lumped together with the Hebrew, often sec­ tarian texts also found at Khirbet Qumran: the Aramaic texts represent their own literary tradition. Nor must they be subordinated to Mesopotamian sci­ entific traditions: the Aramaic texts represent a scientific imagination that, although influenced by Mesopotamia, produced its own innovations.

Released in 2022, Science in Qumran Aramaic Texts is the first volume in the new (indeed, the second volume was only released this year) series Ancient Cultures of Sciences and Knowledge. A glance at the editorial and advisory boards will reveal that the series intends to move beyond more technical histories of science to incorporate social and religious contexts. For example, Paul J. Kosmin (Department of Classics, Harvard) is a historian who has emphasized the social (especially imperial) contexts of spatial and temporal ideology in the Seleucid empire. Jacqueline Vayntrub (Hebrew Bible, Yale Divinity School), in turn, has worked extensively on ancient Israelite poetry and transmission of knowledge. This more elastic approach to methodology and content can be detected in several of the contributions, such as Amar Annus’ chapter, which partly explores the social (i.e., priestly) ramifications of divine doubles, and Jonathan Ben­Dov’s chapter, which critiques current trends in comparative work.

There are 11 distinct chapters (plus the introductory chapter by Ida Fröhlich, the editor), two of which are coauthored. Although entirely in English, the

contributions are relatively international in scope, with authors hailing from Brazil, Israel, the United Kingdom, North America, and Eastern Europe. Most comparative work is undertaken with Mesopotamian texts, and As­ syriologists will find familiar territory throughout. Classicists without some background in the Hebrew Bible or ancient Judaism will find fewer entry points, although Geller’s chapter includes Greek medical texts and Dávid’s chapter concludes with a call for comparisons of Greek and Latin travel lit­ erature. Several chapters, such as Jacobus’ on 4Q208–209, include extremely technical discussions, which could be daunting to those without sufficient background in ancient astronomy but which will nevertheless be warmly received by historians of science. Such historians may initially find several chapters to be less relevant to the history of science (e.g., those on ques­ tions of composition or interpretation primarily of interest to philologists). However, Ida Fröhlich’s introductory chapter helpfully situates the volume and Qumran itself within the wider traditions of the history of science. Do take note, though, that the science in question is primarily astronomical (although there are some treatments of ancient medical discourses).

In “‘Secular Science’ in Mesopotamia”, Markham J. Geller argues that a bur­ geoning scientific (i.e., clockwork) understanding of the cosmos, thanks to advances in astronomical techniques in Mesopotamia, loosened religious interpretations of planetary phenomena, a shift that also occurred in med­ ical practice. Classicists may be intrigued by Geller’s argument that this same tension between science and religion may be found in Greek sources. Historians of science may be especially interested in how Geller also res­ cues astral medicine by demonstrating its inherent logic and arguing that technical explanations began to replace divine ones.

In “‘The Script of God’—Daniel 5:25 in the Light of Mesopotamian Omen Literature”, Réka Esztári and Ádám Vér argue that the “writing on the wall” scene in Daniel 5 represents an erudite reception of cuneiform learning. The authors argue that «mene, mene, tekel, upharsin» is a nuanced Aramaic back­translation of a cuneiform apodosis involving the overthrow of a king. Biblical scholars will, of course, be especially interested in the authors’ inge­ nious interpretation of the passage, but the chapter also represents just how embedded the authors of the biblical text were in Mesopotamian scholarship. Assyriologists (not to mention those with linguistic interests more broadly) may be especially interested in how Esztári and Vér use Daniel 5 to uncover the reception of cuneiform script’s polyvalency in noncuneiform languages.

In “Symptoms and Symbols, Prayers and Portents: Diagnostic Physiognomy and the Diviner in the Aramaic Prayer of Nabonidus (4Q242)”, Andrew

B. Perrin posits that the unnamed gzr in the aforementioned prayer is a name­ less Judaean diviner—not Daniel. Perrin does not argue that Nabonidus’ condition is subject to physiognomy. Rather, his skin condition functions as an omen that must be interpreted to determine which deity is actually the responsible one. Scholars of medical history may be fascinated by how 4Q242 categorizes diseases and their diagnoses, particularly their inter­ sections with divination. Biblical scholars will be especially interested in Perrin’s stance of not identifying the gzr with Daniel.

In “The Heavenly Counterparts of Adapa and Enoch in Babylonia and Is­ rael”, Amar Annus demonstrates that in some traditions

(1) Oannes/Adapa actually remained in heaven, and (2) the Oannes/Adapa figure had a mirror image in heaven (which was then extended to the priestly class).

Annus then places the heavenly Oannes into conversation with the heavenly form of Enoch and the “divine double” scholarship of Andrei Orlov. Schol­ ars of Second Temple Judaism will be especially intrigued by the existence of divine doubles before Enoch. What some readers could find challenging, though, is Annus’ pivot to a discussion of psychology, out-of-body phenom­ ena, and ecstatic experiences in relation to divine doubles. Nevertheless, Assyriologists and biblical scholars alike will be provoked into fruitful dis­ cussion by this chapter and Annus’ fascinating analysis of less well­known but highly valuable texts.

In “How 4QAstronomical Enocha–b (4Q208–209) Transformed Elements of Late Babylonian Magical Hemerological Texts into a Synchronistic Calen­ dar”, Helen R. Jacobus explores hemerological tablet BRM IV, no. 19, which is from Uruk and dates from the Persian or Hellenistic period, demonstrating how 4Q208–209 adopts features of the micro­zodiac. This is a deeply techni­ cal discussion that historians of astronomy and calendars would find most useful and could be a bit daunting to nonspecialists. But from a wider per­ spective, Jacobus masterfully demonstrates just how embedded the authors of these Aramaic texts were in Mesopotamian scholastic traditions.

In “Jewish Aramaic Science and Mythology: Babylonian or Levantine Her­ itage?” Jonathan Ben­Dov pushes back against the Mesopotamia­centric comparative approach. Ben­Dov demonstrates that the “comparison game” can be played between the Book of the Watchers and a Levantine Philo of Byb­ los just as fruitfully as with Mesopotamian sources. Some readers may be per­ turbed by this use of Philo of Byblos (although Ben­Dov acknowledges the transmission difficulties). However, drawing upon material evidence from Maresha, Ben­Dov demonstrates how Mesopotamian knowledge may have filtered in alongside local developments. In particular, Ben­Dov suggests that

In “Writing Science, Writing Magic: Possible Functions for the Act of Writing. Scientific Knowledge Reflected in 4Q560”, Tupá Guerra argues that grammat­ ical irregularities in 4Q560 may reflect “magical” practices (a term for which Guerra explicitly acknowledges its heuristic purpose). Guerra demonstrates, even drawing upon modern evidence, that the writing of magical practices is not simply a record but a magical practice in and of itself. Pointing to inverted writing in other ancient texts, Guerra suggests that the grammatically “incor­ rect” male­female entities in 4Q560 were intentional. While some readers might not prefer the term “magic”, Guerra produces a very helpful reminder that these Aramaic texts are first and foremost written texts—not Platonic ideals floating outside the cosmos.

In “Enoch at the Ends of the Earth: Horizon­Based Astronomy and the Stars in 1 Enoch 33–36”, Henryk Drawnel argues that Enoch travels to the ends of the Earth precisely because this is the region most suitable for gaining accurate knowledge of the heavens (at least from the perspective of hori­ zon­based astronomy). Thus, Enoch’s knowledge is not simply revelation but firsthand, observational knowledge. For historians of science, this chap­ ter is especially useful for revealing an ancient, emic presentation of how astronomical knowledge was produced.

In “‘From there I traveled to another place.’ (1QEn passim): Geography in 1 Enoch 20–32”, Nóra Dávid argues that real­life geography influenced the depiction of Enoch’s journey. In particular, Dávid considers the similarities between paradise and the places of the dead in locales such as Palmyra and Petra. Dávid concludes with a call to place 1 Enoch’s “travels” into conversation with Greek and even Latin travel literature. Classicists and Second Temple scholars alike may be surprised at just how much overlap exists between their respective texts (especially since 1 Enoch is often siloed as an apocalyptic text).

In “The Provenance and Purpose of the Genesis Apocryphon”, Siam Bhayro and Anne Burberry argue that the Genesis apocryphon was conceptual­ ized—in their construction, an important distinction from composed: both Bhayro and Burberry acknowledge that the Aramaic of the actual document points to a Levantine composition—in Mesopotamia rather than in the Lev­ ant as commonly maintained. After carefully rebutting usual arguments in favor of its Levantine conceptualization, they note how the narratives’ emphasis on bloodlines fits better in a diasporic context. This chapter, while sure to provoke responses, is nuanced and deserves attention.

In “Authorizing Knowledge: Magical Healing and the Watchers’ Tradition in Qumran”, Ida Fröhlich explores the intersection of demonology and healing practices at Qumran, demonstrating how the myth of the Watchers provides the conceptual background for the disease/demon nexus found in many Qumran texts. This chapter is an excellent reminder that praxis and Enochic narrative were not siloed from each other in the ancient world.

Perhaps the only substantial issue with the volume is the organization of these diverse chapters. Although the volume contains only 11 chapters (which are, to be clear, not insignificant in length) beyond the introduc­ tion, the rationale presented in the introduction for the chapters’ order­ ing is not always useful in practice. For example, Geller’s opening chap­ ter on astronomical phenomena is immediately followed by a chapter on cuneiform writing and divination, despite the fact that the later chapters of Jacobus and Drawnel (which are themselves not clustered together!) also focus on astronomical phenomena. Similarly, given that Ben­Dov critiques Mesopotamian­centric comparative work, this chapter perhaps would have served as a useful framing piece either at the beginning or end rather than in the middle. The end result is that the reader must jump around a bit if they wish to place related chapters (at least, in my mind) in conversation with one another.

I suspect that some specialists might also have concerns with the use of “sci­ ence” in an ancient context. In my opinion, however, it is refreshing to see the authors refuse to derail into extensive discussions of semantics; they acknowledge that ancient and modern definitions of science differ, and they simply use the term “science” as a heuristic label for the categories of know­ ledge that ancient peoples found relevant—even if that knowledge includes “unscientific” categories such as demonology. In short, as the preface pro­ claims, the authors prefer emic definitions, and yet they avoid reinventing the wheel with new etic terminology. What may be a bit more troubling to some schools of thought in religious studies is the use of “magic” in several chapters and even the category of religion when applied to the ancient world.

In summary, these are minor quibbles, and I heartily recommend this vol­ ume. Scholars interested in the Dead Sea Scrolls, apocalyptic literature, an­ cient Jewish knowledge, and Late Babylonia will find this volume a treasure trove of useful information and provocative ideas. For scholars outside the cosmos of biblical studies and more in history of science proper, a number of these chapters are incredibly relevant for ancient astronomy and medi­ cine, and Fröhlich’s introductory chapter demonstrates why historians of science should care about these Aramaic texts from Qumran.

# MAPK signaling links BRD2 chromatin occupancy to PI3K/AKT inhibitor sensitivity

**Authors:** Josefina Mendez; Simone Bruno; Alexandra Indeglia; Tashbib Khan; Isabella L Ranieri; Jingchao Wang; Jenny Högström; Alissandra L Hillis; Jonah Lee; John G Clohessy; Taru Muranen; Wenyi Wei; Franziska Michor; Karen M Cichowski; Alex Toker

## Abstract

Bromodomain and extra-terminal (BET) proteins, BRD2, BRD3, BRD4, and BRDT, couple histone acetylation to transcription by recruiting elongation and transcription factor complexes to chromatin. Although BET proteins are promising therapeutic targets, the functions of individual family members remain incompletely understood. We identify BRD2 as a co-targetable vulnerability with PI3K/AKT inhibition in breast cancer. Pan-BET inhibition and BRD2 knockout synergized with PI3K pathway inhibitors in breast cancer cell lines, patient-derived organoids, and in vivo models. BRD2 knockout impaired proliferation of triple-negative breast cancer cells and upregulated signaling and stress-response pathways, including the DNA damage response. Mechanistically, BRD2 is phosphorylated at Ser37 by the mitogen-and stress-activated kinases MSK and RSK, and Ser37 phosphorylation is required for chromatin binding and reader function. Finally, mechanistic digital twin modeling identified BETi–PI3Ki regimens that maintained efficacy while reducing drug exposure. Together, these findings identify BRD2 as a phosphorylation-dependent, co-targetable vulnerability in PI3K-inhibited breast cancer.

# ZNF280A links DNA double-strand break repair to human 22q11.2 distal deletion syndrome

**Authors:** Thomas L. Clarke; Hyo Min Cho; Ilaria Ceppi; Boya Gao; Tribhuwan Yadav; Giorgia G. Silveira; Ruben Boon; Barbara Martinez-Pastor; Nana Yaa A. ## Abstract

DNA double-strand breaks (DSB) are among the most deleterious forms of DNA damage and, if unresolved, result in DNA mutations and chromosomal aberrations that can cause disease, including cancer. Repair of DSBs by homologous recombination requires extensive nucleolytic digestion of DNA ends in a process known as DNA-end resection. In recent years, progress has been made in understanding how this process is initiated, but the later stages of this process—long-range DNA-end resection—are not well understood. Many questions remain in terms of how the DNA helicases and endonucleases that catalyse this process are regulated, a key step to avoiding spurious activity in the absence of breaks. The importance of DNA-end resection in human disease is highlighted by several human genetic syndromes that are caused by mutations or deficiencies in key proteins involved in this process. Here, using high-throughput microscopy coupled with a cDNA ‘chromORFeome’ library, we identified ZNF280A as an uncharacterized chromatin factor that is recruited to breaks and essential for DNA DSB repair. Lack of ZNF280A drives genomic instability and substantial sensitivity to DNA-damaging agents. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that ZNF280A promotes long-range DNA-end resection by facilitating the recruitment of the BLM–DNA2 helicase–nuclease complex to DNA DSB sites, enhancing efficiency of the enzymatic activity of this complex at DNA damage sites. ZNF280A is therefore essential for DNA-end resection and DNA repair by homologous recombination. Importantly, ZNF280A is hemizygously deleted in a human genetic condition, 22q11.2 distal deletion syndrome. Features of this condition include congenital heart disease, microcephaly, immune deficiency, developmental delay and cognitive deficits—features that are associated with other human syndromes caused by defects in genes involved in DNA repair. Remarkably, cells from individuals with a 22q11.2 distal deletion have defects in DNA-end resection and homologous recombination, resulting in increased incidence of genomic instability. These phenotypes are rescued by reintroduction of ZNF280A, providing evidence of defective DNA repair as a potential mechanistic explanation for several clinical features associated with this human condition.

Cells are constantly subjected to DNA damage from a range of endogenous and environmental sources, and it is estimated that cells can experience as many as 105 DNA lesions per day1. The accurate repair of this myriad of lesions is critical to preventing genomic instability in the form of mutations and chromosomal aberrations, which can underpin a wide range of pathologies including cancer, immune deficiency, premature ageing and neurodegeneration2. To respond to the array of DNA lesions that occur, cells have developed a complex and coordinated series of steps involving DNA damage recognition, cell cycle arrest and signalling-induced activation of the DNA repair machinery—processes collectively referred to as the DNA damage response (DDR)1,3. Highlighting the importance of the DDR, mutations or deficiency in key components of the DDR are known to cause several human genetic syndromes associated with premature ageing and early onset of malignancy2,4.

One of the most deleterious types of DNA lesion is the DNA double-strand break (DSB), and just one unrepaired DNA DSB may be enough to cause cell death5. Therefore, the presence of DNA DSBs is a genomic emergency in cells. Cells have developed two major DNA repair pathways that repair DNA DSBs, non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) and homologous recombination (HR)1,6. One of the earliest responses to DNA DSBs is the recruitment of DNA damage sensor proteins and complexes such as poly ADP-ribose polymerase-1 (PARP1) and the MRE11–RAD50–NBS1 (MRN) complex1,7. These recruitment events in turn recruit the critical DNA repair protein kinase, ATM, to break sites, where it phosphorylates a number of key substrates to further activate DNA repair signalling cascades, including the histone variant H2A.X on serine 139 (referred to as γH2AX)6,8. This event is critical for propagation of the DDR. Whether cells utilize NHEJ or HR will depend on several factors. NHEJ can occur during all phases of the cell cycle with the exception of mitosis and involves limited end processing of DNA break ends. Instead, break ends are bound by the Ku70/80 heterodimer and protected from nucleolytic digestion by the 53BP1–Shieldin complex9–12. 53BP1 is recruited through two histone marks, H4K20me2 and H2AK15Ub (catalysed by the E3 ubiquitin ligases RNF8 and RNF168)13–16. The 53BP1–RIF-1, REV7–Shieldin complex functions to protect DNA ends from nucleolytic processing, promoting repair of DNA DSBs by NHEJ10–12,17. NHEJ occurs rapidly and without the use of a homologous DNA template. As a result, it has an increased propensity to result in genomic instability, due to the risk of genomic insertions and deletions occurring at the DNA breakpoint.

By contrast, HR primarily utilizes a sister chromatid as a homologous template and is therefore considered to be a more accurate method for resolving DNA DSBs. However, due to the requirement of a sister chromatid, this repair pathway is limited to late S and G2 phase of the cell cycle6. In addition, a prerequisite for HR is the 5′-to-3′ nucleolytic degradation of double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) ends to generate single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) via a tightly regulated process known as DNA-end resection. To enable end-resection initiation, the 53BP1–Shieldin complex must be removed from the DNA DSB site, and this occurs in a dynamic, cell-cycle-dependent manner facilitated in part by histone modification changes including Tip60-mediated histone 4 lysine 16 acetylation (H4K16ac)18,19. DNA resection can be separated into two main steps, DNA resection-initiation/short-range DNA resection and long-range DNA-end resection20. Short-range DNA-end resection is pre-dominantly catalysed by the nuclease MRE11, part of the MRN complex in mammalian cells. A critical co-factor for the MRN complex is CtIP, which enables cell-cycle-dependent regulation of DNA-end resection and HR21–23. Mre11 catalyses the nucleolytic degradation of DNA, generating a short patch of ssDNA, which is believed to serve as a docking site for the long-range nucleases EXO1 and DNA2, the latter of which works in conjunction with the helicase Bloom (BLM) or Werner (WRN)20,24,25. The generation of ssDNA then serves as a substrate for the DNA recombinase RAD51, which promotes strand invasion to start HR repair20. In recent years, a detailed understanding of the regulation of short-range DNA resection has evolved, with the 53BP1–Shieldin complex emerging as a major gate keeper of DNA resection initiation10–12,17. In addition, other critical mediators of short-range resection have also been identified, including DYNLL1, which reduces MRE11 recruitment to DNA DSB sites26. However, it is less clear how long-range DNA-end resection is controlled, in particular, how the helicases and nucleases are regulated to balance the need for efficient enzymatic action at DNA DSB sites without compromising genome integrity via spurious nuclease activity in the context of non-DSBs ssDNA—for instance, during DNA replication and transcription. In this context, it remains unknown how the helicases and nucleases are recruited to DNA DSB sites and whether this is promoted by the physical structure of DNA, that is, the generation of a small section of ssDNA via MRE11-mediated short-range resection, or whether there is more dynamic, finely tuned mechanistic regulation.

The importance of efficient DNA-end resection for human health is highlighted by several human genetic syndromes that are caused by mutations or deficiencies in genes associated with DNA-end resection2,27. Indeed, many of these syndromes, such as DNA2 Seckel syndrome, Bloom syndrome, Werner’s syndrome and CtIP-linked Seckel and Jawad syndromes, exhibit similar clinical features including cognitive impairment, developmental delay, immune deficiency, premature ageing and microcephaly27–29. Interestingly, patients with the human genetic disorder 22q11.2 distal deletion syndrome exhibit many of these same clinical characteristics, raising the possibility that individuals with 22q11.2 distal deletion could also exhibit evidence of genomic instability30. Importantly, the exact genes responsible for these clinical phenotypes in those with 22q11.2 distal deletions remained unknown. Here, using a cDNA ‘chromORFeome’ library coupled with high-throughput microscopy (HTM), we have identified the uncharacterized zinc-finger-containing protein ZNF280A, as a regulator of DNA DSB repair by HR. Our study identifies ZNF280A as a critical mediator of long-range DNA-end resection via recruitment and activation of the essential BLM–DNA2 complex and links the absence of ZNF280A to genomic instability and several clinical features associated with 22q11.2 distal deletion syndrome.

## Results

### ZNF280A facilitates DNA DSB repair

To identify chromatin factors recruited to sites of DNA damage, we have recently developed a high-throughput screening methodology coupled with a custom-made cDNA chromORFeome library of genes predicted to interact with chromatin, based on their sequence and binding motifs31. Using this screening approach coupled with HTM, we identified many known DNA repair factors, as well as several uncharacterized chromatin factors that are recruited to sites of DNA damage, including a zinc-finger-containing protein of unknown function, ZNF280A (Fig. 1a). To confirm the recruitment of ZNF280A to sites of ultraviolet (UV)-laser-induced DNA damage, using lentiviral infection we generated a new stable U2OS cell line expressing V5-tagged ZNF280A and exposed these cells to 405-nm UV-laser microirradiation, followed by fixation approximately 30 min after microirradiation (Fig. 1b). Using this cell line model, we confirmed the recruitment of ectopically expressed V5–ZNF280A to sites of UV-laser-induced DNA damage as measured by colocalization with a γH2AX laser stripe (Fig. 1c and Extended Data Fig. 1b). To further validate this finding, we utilized the U2OS Lac1–Fok1 DNA DSB system18. This cell line expresses an mCherry–Lac1–Fok1 enzyme with both a degradation and an estrogen receptor (ER) domain. Upon addition of Shield-1 and 4-hydroxytamoxifen (4-OHT), Fok1 is stabilized and translocated to the nucleus, where it generates a cluster of site-specific DNA DSBs within LacO repeats that can then be visualized via immunofluorescence (IF) staining and microscopy (Fig. 1d). Using this approach coupled with a ZNF280A antibody, we demonstrated a clear colocalization of endogenous ZNF280A with the classic DNA DSB marker 53BP1 (Fig. 1e,f). To complement these approaches and further validate the recruitment of endogenous ZNF280A protein to DNA damage sites, we performed chromatin fractionation experiments in both U2OS and HeLa cells after exposure to ionizing radiation. Here, we observed clear enrichment of ZNF280A endogenous protein in the chromatin fraction between 45 min and 1 h, after ionizing radiation (Fig. 1g and Extended Data Fig. 1c). Interestingly, the recruitment kinetics of ZNF280A to chromatin following DNA damage appeared to be quite dynamic. To confirm these observations, we performed live cell imaging in U2OS cells expressing a GFP–ZNF280A construct. This analysis demonstrated that GFP–ZNF280A is recruited to sites of DNA damage within the first 5 min of DNA damage induction, with maximal recruitment of ZNF280A approximately 30 min after DNA damage induction. Interestingly, most ZNF280A was removed by 2 h after DNA damage induction, implying that ZNF280A may be functioning at the DNA damage site in the early or mid-stages of the DDR (Fig. 1h,i). Taken together, these data demonstrate that ZNF280A protein is recruited to sites of DNA damage generated by several DNA damaging agents (UV microirradiation, Fok1 DSB and ionizing radiation).

Given the recruitment of ZNF280A protein to DNA damage sites including DNA DSBs (Fig. 1d,e), we reasoned that ZNF280A could be required for the repair of DNA DSBs. To test this hypothesis, we performed clonogenic survival assays in cells that were depleted of ZNF280A using short interfering (si)RNA after exposure to both ionizing radiation and etoposide, a topoisomerase II inhibitor that, like ionizing radiation, is known to generate DNA DSBs32 (Fig. 2a–d). Consistent with a role for ZNF280A in the repair of DNA DSBs, cells depleted of ZNF280A had markedly reduced survival in response to these DNA-damaging agents. To further assess the importance of ZNF280A for DNA repair, we performed γH2AX and 53BP1 time-course experiments to measure DNA-damage-induced foci in response to 3 Gy of ionizing radiation. Notably, ZNF280A-depleted cells had significantly slower kinetics of 53BP1 removal (Fig. 2e,f), and elevated levels of γH2AX 24 h after ionizing radiation compared with cells transfected with a non-targeting siRNA control (Fig. 2g,h and Extended Data Fig. 2a–e). Importantly, this effect on γH2AX foci resolution could be completely rescued by reconstitution with a wild-type ZNF280A cDNA, excluding the possibility that these results could be caused by siRNA off-target effects (Fig. 2g,h and Extended Data Fig. 2e).

Unresolved DNA damage can result in wide-spread genomic instability that can be visualized using microscopy. Two such examples are 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI)-positive micronuclei, which are extranuclear bodies that contain damaged chromosome fragments, and chromosomal aberrations in metaphases33. Interestingly, ZNF280A-depleted HeLa cells exhibited increased incidences of micronuclei after ionizing radiation and elevated levels of 53BP1 foci (Fig. 2i–k), consistent with earlier results in U2OS cells (Fig. 2e,f and Extended Data Fig. 2f). In addition, ZNF280A-depleted HeLa cells exhibit significantly increased chromosomal aberrations per metaphase after ionizing radiation (Fig. 2l–m and Extended Data Fig. 2g). Taken together, these data demonstrate a critical role for ZNF280A in the resolution of DNA DSBs, one of the most deleterious forms of DNA damage, and suggests that the absence of ZNF280A results in substantially elevated levels of genomic instability.

### ZNF280A is a key mediator of HR

As mentioned above, DNA DSBs are repaired by two major DNA repair pathways in mammalian cells, NHEJ and HR. NHEJ involves minimal processing of DNA DSB ends, and the relatively simple ligation of DNA breaks to repair the lesion, but increased risk of genomic instability because of the elevated likelihood of genomic deletions and insertions occurring at the DNA breakpoint. To address this issue, cells have developed a more complex repair process involving extensive resection of broken DNA ends and use of a homologous DNA template to facilitate error-free repair of complex replication-associated DNA DSBs via HR. Given the timing of ZNF280A recruitment to sites of DNA damage (Fig. 1c–i), we reasoned that ZNF280A was more likely to be involved in repair of DNA DSBs via HR as opposed to the more rapidly utilized NHEJ. To test this, we evaluated the localization of the key recombinase Rad51, which is essential for the HR repair pathway6. Given that HR occurs during late S/G2 phase of the cell cycle, we performed IF co-staining of Rad51 and the late S/G2 phase marker mitosin. Cells in late S/G2 phase will have increased mitosin intensity compared with G1-phase cells (Extended Data Fig. 3q), thereby enabling quantification of Rad51 foci specifically when HR is utilized. Interestingly, mitosin-positive (late S/G2 phase) U2OS cells depleted of ZNF280A had markedly reduced localization of Rad51 protein 6 h after ionizing radiation (Fig. 3a–c and Extended Data Fig. 3a–d), and this was also recapitulated in HeLa cells depleted of ZNF280A (Extended Data Fig. 3g,h). Importantly, Rad51 foci localization could be restored in ZNF280A-depleted cells by reconstitution with wild-type ZNF280A cDNA (Fig. 3d,e and Extended Data Fig. 3e,f,i). To directly measure HR efficiency in ZNF280A-depleted cells, we utilized the DR–GFP U2OS HR reporter cell line. Transfection of an I-Sce-1 enzyme generates a site-specific DNA DSB within the GFP transgene expressed in these cells. Repair of the DNA DSB via HR restores the expression of this transgene, promoting the expression of GFP signal. This system therefore enables the direct quantification of HR efficiency by measuring GFP expression using flow cytometry. Consistent with defective Rad51 foci formation, using the DR–GFP reporter system, we directly demonstrated that depletion of ZNF280A dramatically reduces HR efficiency (Fig. 3f,g and Extended Data Fig. 3p).

To further substantiate this finding, we performed clonogenic survival assays in response to the PARP inhibitor olaparib. Olaparib inhibits the repair of ssDNA breaks, which causes conflict with the DNA replication machinery during the following S phase, ultimately leading to DNA replication fork collapse and DNA DSBs in S phase that must be repaired by HR34,35. Therefore, sensitivity to olaparib is indicative of defects in HR-mediated repair. This notion of synthetic lethality has been successfully exploited in the clinic in recent years in the context of BRCA1/2-deficient breast, ovarian and pancreatic tumours that are defective in HR36,37. Confirming a critical role for ZNF280A in HR-mediated repair, U2OS and HeLa cells depleted of ZNF280A exhibited exquisite sensitivity to olaparib treatment (Fig. 3h,i and Extended Data Fig. 3j,k), and importantly, reconstitution of wild-type ZNF280A cDNA was able to completely rescue sensitivity to olaparib in ZNF280A-depleted cells (Extended Data Fig. 3l,m). Cells defective in HR will often attempt to compensate by overutilizing non-homologous end joining in an attempt to repair complex, DNA replication-associated DNA DSBs. Indeed, this often manifests in the aberrant end joining of multiple broken chromosomes38. Consistent with this, ZNF280A-depleted HeLa cells exhibit increases in the number of radial chromosomes per metaphase 24 h after ionizing radiation—indicating an attempt to compensate for defective HR repair, further solidifying a role for ZNF280A in the repair of DNA DSBs via HR (Extended Data Fig. 3n,o).

### ZNF280A is a critical facilitator of DNA-end resection

Given the robust defective HR phenotypes in the absence of ZNF280A, we next assessed whether it may influence DNA-end resection, a key prerequisite for HR. Resection initiation is well understood, with the identification of the Shieldin DNA repair complex, which acts as a crucial gate keeper of DNA DSB repair pathway choice by limiting DNA-end resection initiation20. By contrast, how long-range DNA-end resection is controlled, and in particular how some of the key enzymes, including the helicases BLM and WRN and nucleases DNA2 and EXO1, are regulated, remains a key question in the DNA repair field. To begin to understand if ZNF280A is involved in regulating DNA-end resection as a possible mechanistic explanation for its importance for HR, we measured RPA70 foci levels after ionizing radiation in mitosin-positive late S- and G2-phase cells. ssDNA is coated by the replication protein A (RPA) complex, which facilitates its stabilization and protects ssDNA from degradation, providing a binding platform for the recruitment of the critical recombinase Rad51. Consistent with a role for ZNF280A in DNA-end resection, ZNF280A-depleted mitosin-positive cells had significantly reduced levels of RPA70 foci formation 6 h after ionizing radiation (Fig. 4a,b and Extended Data Fig. 4a), and this could be completely rescued by complementation with wild-type ZNF280A cDNA (Fig. 4c,d and Extended Data Fig. 3i). In agreement with a reduction in ssDNA generation, ZNF280A-depleted cells had notably reduced RPA phosphorylation at serine 4 and 8, as measured by immunoblot analysis of chromatin fractions after ionizing radiation (Fig. 4e). These results were also confirmed after treatment with the topoisomerase I inhibitor camptothecin (Extended Data Fig. 4b–e). To further assess the extent of ssDNA generation via DNA-end resection, we also performed a native bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU) labelling experiment. HeLa cells treated with either a non-targeting siRNA control or two independent ZNF280A-targeted siRNA sequences were labelled with BrdU for approximately 36 h, followed by a 4-h treatment with 1 μM camptothecin. Camptothecin, a topoisomerase I inhibitor, generates SSBs leading to DSBs in S phase by disrupting the progression of the DNA replication fork machinery1. IF staining with a BrdU antibody was then performed with the rationale that the BrdU antibody will recognize BrdU-labelled nascent DNA only if DNA is single-stranded as a result of DNA-end resection after camptothecin-induced DNA damage (Extended Data Fig. 4f). Strikingly, ZNF280A-depleted cells had significantly reduced BrdU signal after camptothecin treatment compared with HeLa cells treated with a non-targeting siRNA (Fig. 4f,g).

RPA-labelled ssDNA, in addition to acting as a binding platform for Rad51, can also act as a platform for the recruitment of the ATR–ATRIP complex. ATR–ATRIP can bind RPA and activate the ATR–CHK1 replication stress axis to promote checkpoint inhibition, pausing cell cycle progression and thus allowing time for DNA repair to take place39. In further agreement with a role for ZNF280A in the generation of ssDNA after DNA damage, phosphorylation of the direct downstream ATR substrate, Chk1 (at serine 345), is markedly diminished in ZNF280A-depleted cells after treatment with camptothecin (Fig. 4h), and late S/G2-phase mitosin-positive cells also exhibit more DNA damage in the absence of ZNF280A (Extended Data Fig. 4h,i). To directly measure and quantify ssDNA formation in ZNF280A-depleted cells, we used the AsiSI–U2OS model system (AsiSI is an isoschizomer of the SfaAI restriction enzyme)40, which has been used to assess end resection in cells. In this system, the addition of 4-OHT causes the AsiSI enzyme to translocate from the cytoplasm to the nucleus where it then generates a site-specific DNA DSB. Genomic DNA is then isolated, and a DNA digest is performed with the restriction enzyme BsrG1. In the absence of DNA-end resection, the genomic DNA is double-stranded and undergoes efficient digestion with the BsrG1 enzyme. However, the presence of ssDNA after DNA-end resection reduces the efficiency of the BsrG1 digest, and as a result, PCR amplification with primers downstream of the AsiSI site is enabled38 (Fig. 4i). Strikingly, this assay revealed that ZNF280A depletion results in the reduction of ssDNA at AsiSI-induced site-specific DNA DSB sites, to a similar extent as that of BRCA1 depletion (Fig. 4j and Extended Data Fig. 4g). Lastly, and further validating ZNF280A’s critical roles in DNA-end resection and HR, HeLa and U2OS cells depleted of ZNF280A with two independent siRNA sequences and an shRNA sequence demonstrated exquisite sensitivity to camptothecin in clonogenic survival assays (Fig. 4k–l and Extended Data Fig. 4j–n), whereas overexpression of ZNF280A in U2OS cells actually enhanced Rad51 foci after ionizing radiation and conferred resistance to camptothecin treatment (Extended Data Fig. 4o–r), which is consistent with data correlating high expression of ZNF280A with chemoradiotherapy resistance in certain cancer contexts41. Together these data demonstrate that ZNF280A promotes DNA DSB repair by promoting the efficient generation of ssDNA via DNA-end resection, facilitating HR-mediated repair.

### ZNF280A interacts with BLM–DNA2 to facilitate long-range DNA-end resection

To begin to understand the mechanism by which ZNF280A may be facilitating DNA-end resection, we performed an in vitro binding assay with recombinant ZNF280A protein and either a 63-nucleotide length of ssDNA or a 55-bp length of dsDNA. Strikingly, ZNF280A had a substantially increased binding affinity for ssDNA compared with dsDNA (Fig. 5a–c). As mentioned previously, DNA-end resection occurs in two phases. DNA resection is initially catalysed by the enzymes CtIP and MRE11 acting with the MRN complex, whereby they first generate nicks in the 5′ terminated DNA strand, ultimately leading to a 3′-terminated ssDNA overhang around 100 nucleotides in length20. Based on our in vitro DNA binding assay, we hypothesized that ZNF280A was functioning downstream of MRN and CtIP in DNA-end resection. Consistent with this hypothesis, ZNF280A depletion had no impact on the recruitment of Mre11 to a Fok1-induced DNA DSB (Extended Data Fig. 5a–c) or on Mre11 foci formation after ionizing radiation (Extended Data Fig. 5d). By contrast, depletion of MRE11 or CtIP completely impaired ZNF280A enrichment in the chromatin fraction after ionizing radiation (Fig. 5d and Extended Data Fig. 5e,f), confirming that Mre11 and CtIP function upstream of ZNF280A in response to DNA DSBs and further suggesting that ZNF280A was probably functioning in the later stages of DNA-end resection. To begin to address this question, we performed endogenous co-immunoprecipitation experiments with the helicases BLM and WRN and the nucleases DNA2 and EXO1, all key enzymes during long-range DNA-end resection20. Notably, we saw robust interaction between ZNF280A and both DNA2 and BLM (Fig. 5e,f), but not EXO1 or WRN. Importantly, reciprocal immunoprecipitation experiments using V5-tagged ZNF280A also confirmed these protein–protein interactions (Extended Data Fig. 5g,h). In addition, we were able to demonstrate an increase in BLM and ZNF280A interaction after ionizing radiation, suggesting a dynamic interaction that is enhanced upon DNA damage (Extended Data Fig. 5i). To investigate the importance of this interaction further and determine the importance of ZNF280A for the recruitment of the BLM–DNA2 complex to DNA DSB sites, we assessed the ability of cells to recruit DNA2 to a Fok1-induced DNA DSB, both in the presence and in the absence of ZNF280A. Strikingly, depletion of ZNF280A significantly reduced the localization of DNA2 to DNA DSB sites, suggesting a dependence on ZNF280A for the recruitment of the critical DNA2–BLM complex to DNA damage sites (Fig. 5g,h). To explore this in more detail, we performed epistasis experiments measuring the relationship between ZNF280A and DNA2-BLM in the context of olaparib sensitivity. Interestingly, double depletion of both ZNF280A and BLM or DNA2 resulted in no additional sensitivity to olaparib, despite individual siRNA knockdowns of each gene exhibiting significant cellular sensitivity (Fig. 5i,j and Extended Data Fig. 5j–m). To further confirm this epistatic relationship in the context of DNA damage, we wanted to assess the impact of double depletion of ZNF280A and DNA2 for Rad51 foci formation after ionizing radiation. Previous reports have indicated that depletion of DNA2 results in a significant reduction in Rad51 foci formation and defects in HR after exposure to ionizing radiation42. Consistent with these reports, in our experiments, siRNA depletion of DNA2 also dramatically reduced Rad51 foci formation in U2OS cells. Importantly, depletion of ZNF280A reduced Rad51 foci formation to similar levels as DNA2 depletion, and double depletion had no additional effect (Extended Data Fig. 5n–p). Taken together, these data demonstrate a complete epistatic relationship between ZNF280A and DNA2–BLM for HR-mediated repair of DNA DSBs and suggests that ZNF280A dynamically regulates the recruitment of DNA2–BLM to facilitate long-range DNA-end resection. To better understand the structure function relationship between ZNF280A and BLM–DNA2, we generated a series of Flag-tagged ZNF280A truncation constructs and performed immunoprecipitation from cells (Fig. 5k and Extended Data Fig. 4s). This analysis revealed that BLM interacts with ZNF280A within the first 100 amino acids of ZNF280A protein (Fig. 5k). In addition, we also generated a ZNF280A construct that lacked its four C2H2 zinc finger domains. This construct was relatively unstable and expressed at lower levels compared with wild-type ZNF280A; nonetheless, this construct still interacted with BLM, indicating that the C2H2 zinc finger domains of ZNF280A are dispensable for its interaction with the BLM–DNA2 complex. Importantly, a ZNF280A BLM binding mutant (ZNF280A Δ1–200) and a ZNF280A C2H2 zinc finger mutant both demonstrated impaired RPA70 and Rad51 foci formation after ionizing radiation, indicating that the ability of ZNF280A to bind both BLM–DNA2 and DNA is critical for its role in DNA DSB repair (Fig. 5l–m and Extended Data Fig. 5q,r).

To directly address how ZNF280A promotes DNA-end resection, we performed a series of in vitro biochemical assays to assess the impact of ZNF280A on BLM and DNA2 enzymatic function. First, we wanted to determine whether ZNF280A has any intrinsic helicase activity that may help to facilitate long-range DNA-end resection. To assess this, we used an oligonucleotide-based Y-structured DNA substrate and assessed the ability of ZNF280A recombinant protein to catalyse the unwinding of this substrate to generate ssDNA in vitro29 (Extended Data Fig. 5s). This experiment demonstrated that ZNF280A alone has no inherent enzymatic activity to promote the unwinding of dsDNA. However, when ZNF280A was added into the same reaction with recombinant BLM, there was a robust increase in the extent of BLM-mediated unwinding of the short Y-structured DNA substrate compared with the condition with BLM alone (Extended Data Fig. 5t,u). If ZNF280A enhances the DNA unwinding capabilities of BLM in vitro, we reasoned that ZNF280A recombinant protein may also enhance the efficiency of long-range DNA-end resection in vitro. To this point, we used a 2-kb-long double-stranded 32P-randomly labelled DNA substrate and assessed the ability of BLM and DNA2 in combination with ZNF280A recombinant protein, to resect this substrate in the presence of the single-stranded DNA binding protein RPA29. Under these conditions, we did not observe further stimulation of BLM-dependent DNA unwinding by ZNF280A (Fig. 5n, lanes 2–5) but found that the DNA-end resection activity of the BLM–DNA2–RPA complex was stimulated more than 2-fold (Fig. 5n,o, lanes 6–9). Supplementing the reactions containing BLM, DNA2 and RPA led to more DNA substrate being utilized, resulting in a concomitant increase of DNA degradation products migrating at the bottom of the gel (compare lanes 6 and 7 in Fig. 5n). Given that this is an in vitro system using recombinant protein substrates, this result indicates a direct effect of ZNF280A on the function of the BLM–DNA helicase–nuclease ensemble. Therefore, taken together, our data demonstrate that ZNF280A regulates long-range DNA-end resection in response to DNA DSBs via BLM–DNA2, probably by increasing BLM–DNA2 recruitment to ssDNA at DNA damage sites—thereby enhancing the efficiency of the helicase and nuclease activities of the BLM–DNA2 complex. This dynamic relationship ultimately promotes efficient long-range DNA-end resection, which is a critical prerequisite for the repair of DNA DSBs by HR.

### ZNF280A is deleted in human 22q11.2 distal deletion syndrome

Our results so far demonstrate that ZNF280A is an important regulator of long-range DNA-end resection by enhancing the enzymatic function of the BLM–DNA2 complex in response to DNA DSBs. Interestingly, deficiency or mutations in several genes that encode proteins that facilitate DNA-end resection are implicated in human genetic syndromes27. Examples of these syndromes include DNA2-linked Seckel syndrome, Bloom syndrome and Werner’s syndrome2,27,43. Importantly, some of the key clinical characteristics of these human syndromes include premature ageing, skeletal defects, immune deficiency, developmental delay, cognitive impairment, microcephaly and an increased risk of malignancy. Given our uncovered role for ZNF280A in DNA-end resection, we reasoned that it was possible that ZNF280A may too be implicated in a human genetic syndrome.

The ZNF280A gene resides within the 22q11.2 region (LCR22D–LCR22E, where LCR stands for locus control region), distal to the classic 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (LCR22A–LCR22D), which is the most common cause of DiGeorge syndrome (Fig. 6a). Notably, this more distal LCR22D–LCR22E region is deleted in a human genetic syndrome known as 22q11.2 distal deletion syndrome30,44. Patients with the 22q11.2 LCR22D–LCR22E deletion have clinical features including microcephaly, immune deficiency, developmental delay and cognitive deficits—all of which, as mentioned above, are classic clinical features seen in several other human conditions caused by defects in genes that are involved in DNA repair2,27,44 (Supplementary Table 1). Of note, patients with the more prevalent proximal deletion that does not include ZNF280A (LCR22A–LCR22D)—the so-called Di George syndrome—present less frequently with microcephaly, short stature and global developmental delay (Fig. 6a,b, Extended Data Fig. 6a–e and Supplementary Tables 1–4). Importantly, the underlying causes of these clinical features in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome are unknown.

To investigate the link between ZNF280A and human 22q11.2 distal deletion syndrome (LCR22D–LCR22E) in more detail, we obtained patient-derived lymphocyte cell lines from patients with the 22q11.2 LCR22D–LCR22E deletion. Clinical diagnostics using multiplex-ligation dependent probe amplification (from MRC-Holland) were performed on these patients to confirm deletion of one allele at this locus (Extended Data Fig. 6b and Supplementary Tables 2–4). Real-time PCR analysis in these cell lines demonstrated that these cells display haploinsufficiency of ZNF280A, with RNA levels at approximately 50% compared with those of a patient with proximal 22q11.2 deletion (LCR22A–LCR22D; Fig. 6b), and this was corroborated with immunoblot analysis of ZNF280A protein levels (Extended Data Fig. 6a). These cell lines can also be compared with DNA copy number at 50% when compared with a LCR22A–LCR22D patient, which we used as a reference point control for these assays (Extended Data Fig. 6b and Supplementary Tables 2–4). Next, to determine whether the haploinsufficiency of ZNF280A caused by deletion of the 22q11.2 LCR22D–LCR22E region impacted genomic stability in these patients, we measured basal levels of γH2AX and 53BP1, independent of any exogenous DNA damage. Remarkably, patient-derived cell lines with haploinsufficiency of ZNF280A/22q11.2 LCR22D–LCR22E deletion had significantly increased endogenous DNA damage as measured by the number of overlapping γH2AX and 53BP1 foci, compared with the patient with the standard LCR22A–LCR22D deletion with an intact 22q11.2 LCR22D–LCR22E region (Fig. 6c,d and Extended Data Fig. 6k). To further link 22q11.2 LCR22D–LCR22E deletion to defective DNA-end resection and impaired HR, as seen with siRNA depletion of ZNF280A, we exposed patient-derived lymphocytes to ionizing radiation and assessed RPA70 and Rad51 foci localization in these cells. Consistent with our siRNA experiments, patients with intact ZNF280A/22q11.2 (LCR22A–LCR22D deletion) had a robust RPA70 and Rad51 foci response after ionizing radiation. By contrast, cell lines with haploinsufficiency of ZNF280A/22q11.2 (LCR22D–LCR22E) demonstrate a suppressed RPA70 and Rad51 response, indicating defects in DNA-end resection and HR, respectively (Fig. 6e–h and Extended Data Fig. 6l). To confirm that haploinsufficiency of ZNF280A is a major driver of these phenotypes, we generated a ZNF280A partial knockout U2OS cell line (sgZNF280ApKO) using CRISPR–Cas9 (Extended Data Fig. 6f–j). Strikingly, U2OS sgZNF280ApKO cells have significantly reduced RPA70 foci and Rad51 foci formation after ionizing radiation, confirming that haploinsufficiency of ZNF280A is a major driver of defective DNA repair in human cells (Fig. 6i–l).

To conclusively confirm that the haploinsufficiency of ZNF280A was responsible for impaired DNA DSB repair in patient cells, we reconstituted wild-type ZNF280A cDNA into 22q11.2 (LCR22D–LCR22E)-deleted cells derived from patients (patients 2 and 3) and determined whether this could rescue the genomic instability observed in these cells. Strikingly, cells that were successfully nucleofected with V5-tagged ZNF280A exhibited significantly less DNA damage as measured by 53BP1 foci, compared with cells that did not express V5–ZNF280A (Fig. 6m–o). All together, these results provide strong evidence that deletion of ZNF280A in the 22q11.2 LCR22D–LCR22E deletion syndrome may explain the biology underpinning some of the clinical features of these patients (Fig. 6b and Supplementary Table 1), similar to what is observed in other human syndromes of genomic instability.

## Discussion

Using a recently developed chromORFeome library coupled with HTM31, here we have identified an uncharacterized chromatin factor, ZNF280A, that is important for DNA repair. We demonstrate that ZNF280A is critical for facilitating long-range DNA-end resection, an essential prerequisite for HR-mediated repair. Mechanistically, ZNF280A dynamically regulates the recruitment of the BLM–DNA2 helicase–nuclease complex to DNA DSB sites, enhancing the efficiency of their enzymatic function during DNA repair, to catalyse long-range DNA-end resection. Critically, ZNF280A is deleted in a human genetic syndrome—22q11.2 distal deletion syndrome. Clinical features of this condition include immune deficiency, developmental delay, cognitive impairment and microcephaly. Consistent with these clinical features, cell lines derived directly from patients who exhibit haploinsufficiency of ZNF280A have increased genomic instability and defects in DNA-end resection and HR, and these phenotypes are rescued by the reexpression of ZNF280A, directly linking this gene to the clinical manifestations in patients. Therefore, we have identified an uncharacterized chromatin factor, ZNF280A, and directly linked its importance in DNA repair to a human genetic syndrome.

So far, identification of chromatin factors in DNA repair has been limited due to the lack of high-throughput screening methodologies. Moreover, traditional siRNA screens and more recent CRISPR knockout screening approaches have proved challenging in the context of chromatin factors, due to their essentiality for cell viability. Our current study provides strong evidence that our approach exploiting a cDNA chromORFeome library in a high-throughput context has the potential to identify uncharacterized chromatin factors essential for DNA repair that may have been missed via conventional screening approaches. Indeed, ZNF280A has not been previously identified in DNA damage repair screens using knockdown or CRISPR–Cas9 knockout approaches.

Identification of ZNF280A as a critical regulator of the BLM–DNA2 complex addresses a major unanswered question in the DNA repair field. How these critical enzymes involved in catalysing DNA-end resection are regulated has not been fully understood. Our proposed model is consistent with these enzymes having a finely tuned regulatory system, which is necessary to avoid inappropriate helicase and nuclease activity in the absence of DNA damage. This is essential to limit endogenous DNA damage caused by poorly regulated nuclease activity during normal cellular metabolic events such as DNA replication and DNA transcription. The requirement for a small section of ssDNA to be present to facilitate the binding of ZNF280A, which is essential for BLM–DNA2 recruitment, suggests that the initiation of DNA-end resection is a critical requirement for the activation of the ZNF280A–BLM–DNA2 long-range end-resection axis. Our model implies a finely tuned regulatory system including physical DNA structure and a key ssDNA binding intermediate—ZNF280A—as essential regulators of BLM–DNA2-mediated DNA-end resection in the context of DNA DSBs. Interestingly, ZNF280A depletion impairs DNA-end resection and HR to a greater extent than BLM or DNA2 alone. This implies that the single depletion of BLM or DNA2 can be compensated for by redundancy with other helicases and nucleases respectively, whereas the depletion of ZNF280A probably impairs the function of the BLM–DNA2 complex that cannot be compensated for by other enzymes. However, we cannot rule out that there may be additional mechanisms in play. For example, we see increased 53BP1 retention at DNA DSBs upon ZNF280A depletion. It is highly possible that this could also be impacting DNA resection, and further work is needed to provide a complete picture of how ZNF280A regulates DNA DSB repair and genomic integrity maintenance.

In future studies, it will also be important to further understand how ZNF280A itself is regulated. For instance, is the recruitment of ZNF280A to DSB sites a dynamically regulated process or is its recruitment mediated simply by the physical presence of a short section of ssDNA generated by MRE-11 nucleolytic digestion? Understanding these mechanistic nuances will be critical to establishing whether targeting ZNF280A could be a viable therapeutic option in diseases underpinned by genomic instability, such as cancer. In this regard, recent reports have indicated that increased expression of ZNF280A correlates with chemotherapy resistance in colorectal cancer41. Given the uncovered role for ZNF280A in the regulation of DNA repair, it will be important to determine whether ZNF280A expression directly influences the efficiency of DNA repair in the context of cancer, and whether this could impact therapy response in patients. In addition, these studies will also determine whether ZNF280A expression may be helpful in stratifying patients for targeted DNA repair therapies. Indeed, it is becoming clear that the appropriate stratification of patient subpopulations is critical for realizing the potential of targeted therapeutics. For example, a recent study reported a 100% complete clinical response rate in patients with colorectal cancer treated with immune checkpoint blockade, all of whom had mutations driving defects in the mismatch repair DNA repair pathway45. More detailed mechanistic understanding of DNA repair processes will be essential for both the stratification of patients for targeted therapies, as well as for addressing acquired resistance that is often seen in patients treated with better-tolerated, more-targeted cancer therapies46–48.

Human 22q11.2 deletion syndrome is an umbrella term for a range of disorders whose clinical manifestations depend on the size and location of the genomic region deleted. For example, standard deletions of this locus (LCR22A–LCR22D) are the most common cause of DiGeorge syndrome, most frequently resulting in congenital heart disease, immune deficiency, hypoparathyroidism, palatal anomalies and developmental differences30.

ZNF280A resides within the more distally located LCR22D–LCR22E region of 22q11.2 (refs. 30,44). Interestingly, ZNF280A appears to be expressed at low levels in human cells. One study has even reported that the LCR22D-E region, including the ZNF280A gene, is actually deleted in human B cells as a consequence of immunoglobulin lambda light chain rearrangement49, suggesting that, at least in some specific B cells, ZNF280A may have redundant functions with other isoforms. Further studies are therefore needed to better understand the importance of ZNF280A expression and biological function in specific cell and tissue contexts.

Despite relatively low expression of ZNF280A, patients with hemizygous deletion of the LCR22D–LCR22E region, and thus even lower expression of ZNF280A, have a range of clinical features including cognitive impairment, immune deficiency and developmental delay. In addition, many patients with the LCR22D–LCR22E deletion exhibit microcephaly. These clinical features are entirely consistent with other human conditions caused by mutations or deletions in genes known to be important for DNA repair. In addition to these common clinical features, other human syndromes caused by defects in DNA repair genes often confer an increased risk of malignancy. This therefore raises an important question in the context of children with 22q11.2 LCR22D–LCR22E deletions, as to whether they are at increased risk of malignancy. Importantly, among deletions distal to the LCR22D–LCR22E region of 22q11.2, the LCR22F–LCR22G region includes a deletion of the essential tumour suppressor gene SMARCB1, which results in nearly 100% penetrance of rhabdoid sarcoma in children with this deletion50. As a result, children with 22q11.2 distal deletion (LCR22F–LCR22G) are monitored with yearly magnetic resonance imaging to screen for tumour development, as part of routine clinical management of these patients50. Based on our findings that 22q11.2 LCR22D–LCR22E patient-derived cells exhibit defects in DNA-end resection and HR and increased genomic instability, in addition to the other clinical features seen in these patients, it raises the question whether routine clinical imaging and tumour surveillance should be extended to patients with 22q11.2 distal deletion including those proximal to the LCR22F–LCR22G region, specifically LCR22D–LCR22E deletion51. More detailed clinical analysis will be necessary to explore the risk of malignancy in these patients, but our findings described here offer rationale for further study of this important question.

As mentioned above, we find ZNF280A as haploinsufficient in 22q11.2 distal deletion (LCR22D-E) patient-derived cells. Although many DNA repair human syndromes occur as homozygous deletion, several studies have identified other repair haploinsufficiency disorders, including a subset of blepharophimosis–ptosis–epicanthus inversus syndrome, Miller–Dieker lissencephaly syndrome and Williams–Beuren syndrome—in which the deleted region encompasses ATR, RPA1 and RFC2, respectively52. Importantly, like patients with 22q11.2 distal deletion syndrome, patients with the above mentioned haploinsufficient disorders also present with microcephaly, growth delay and impaired cognitive function53–55. All together, these studies indicate that, at least for some factors, even 50% decrease in levels is enough to drive defective DNA repair.

In closing, here we identify an uncharacterized chromatin factor, ZNF280A, as an essential regulator of DNA repair. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that ZNF280A is a key rheostat of the BLM–DNA2 helicase–nuclease complex, regulating its recruitment to DNA DSBs and binding affinity to ssDNA, enhancing the enzymatic activity of the complex at DNA DSB sites and, thus, addressing a long-standing question in the DNA repair field of how these key enzymes are regulated. In addition, we link ZNF280A haploinsufficiency with the manifestations of the 22q11.2 distal deletion (LCR22D–LCR22E) genetic human syndrome and demonstrate that patients with this condition have defective DNA-end resection or HR and increased genomic instability. Importantly, our study offers a rationale for further analysis to understand the risk of malignancy in these patients and provides the first evidence of defective DNA repair as a potential mechanistic explanation for some of the clinical features associated with this human syndrome.
